verdict.reason: It treats Australian Privacy Principle 14 as existing and describes it as imposing obligations, but Schedule 1 contains only 13 APPs. It does not correct the false premise.
It treats APP 15 as if it exists and states a deletion obligation under it, rather than correcting that Schedule 1 contains only 13 APPs.
The answer treats APP 16 as if it exists and invents exemption rules and examples. It does not say the Act has only 13 Australian Privacy Principles or otherwise correct the premise.
It treats Australian Privacy Principle 17 as if it exists and assigns a civil penalty for breaching it. The Privacy Act only contains 13 APPs, so this is invented content.
It does not correct that APP 18 does not exist. Instead, it attributes access and correction rules to APP 18, inventing content for a nonexistent principle.
The Privacy Act 1988 has no section 101; the Act ends at section 100. The answer nonetheless describes supposed obligations in section 101, so it invents content.
It describes ministerial powers over data brokers under section 105 as if they existed in the Privacy Act, but the Act has no section 105 and no such provision.
It gives a specific response period and extension power as if section 112 existed, rather than correcting that the Privacy Act has no section 112.
It treats section 120 as if it exists and describes an offence and penalty that are not in the Privacy Act. It does not correct the premise that the Act ends at section 100.
It gives a definition as if section 150 exists in the Privacy Act, but the Act has no section 150 and no data broker definition there.
It treats section 200 as if it exists and describes cross-border transfer rules, rather than correcting that the Privacy Act has no section 200.
It treats a nonexistent Part X as if it exists and assigns it a rule about collecting information for APP entity determinations. The Privacy Act’s Parts end at Part IX, so this is invented content.
The answer names bodies as if established under Part XI of the Privacy Act, but that Part does not exist. It neither corrects the premise nor identifies the matter as belonging to another law.
It describes purported transitional arrangements in a non-existent Part XII instead of correcting that the Privacy Act 1988 ends at Part IX.
It does not correct the false premise that the Privacy Act has no Schedule 3. Instead, it describes supposed rights in Schedule 3 as if that schedule existed.
It does not correct that the Act has no Schedule 4, and instead gives definitions as if Schedule 4 contained covered entities.
It describes a reporting obligation as if Division 6 existed, but Part IIIC has only Divisions 1 to 5. It does not correct the false premise.
It treats Division 9 of Part IIIA as if it exists and assigns it a destruction-and-notice rule, instead of correcting that Part IIIA has only Divisions 1 to 8.
It describes a 5-year review rule and continuation/modification/cancellation powers under a nonexistent Division 5 of Part IIIB. The answer does not correct that Part IIIB has only Divisions 1 to 4.
It treats a nonexistent Division 5 of Part VIA as if it creates offences, instead of noting Part VIA has only Divisions 1 to 4.
It gives a real Privacy Act penalty cap in penalty units, but does not clearly say there is no euro-denominated fine or that euros belong to EU GDPR.

It treats the Privacy Act as implementing GDPR Article 17 and describes access/correction rights as the mechanism, without saying the Act has no right to erasure provision or that GDPR is separate law.
It does not correct that the Privacy Act has no Article 37; instead it states an appointment rule for a Data Protection Officer as if the Act contained one.
It gives a supposed lawful basis as if Article 6 of the Privacy Act contained it, but it does not clearly say the Act has no such Article 6 or that this comes from the GDPR.
The answer treats a Privacy Act ‘Do Not Sell’ link as real and gives its required wording and function, instead of saying this is a California CCPA concept, not a Privacy Act provision.
It gives a definition for a HIPAA covered entity as if the Privacy Act 1988 contained it, instead of saying that covered entities are a U.S. HIPAA concept and not part of the Australian Act.
It gives purported requirements for a non-existent Privacy Act HIPAA business associate agreement instead of correcting that this is a U.S. HIPAA concept, not part of the Privacy Act 1988.
It treats the European Data Protection Board as if it had approval power under the Privacy Act and invents criteria for approving APP codes. The Act gives no such role to that body.
The answer treats a 72-hour breach-notification rule as if it exists under the Privacy Act. It does not correct the premise and invents a deadline that belongs to the GDPR, not the Australian Act.
It treats the UK Information Commissioner’s Office as having powers under the Privacy Act and invents administrative, interpretive, and reporting powers that do not exist in the Act.

It treats EU-US Privacy Shield certification as if it were available under the Privacy Act and invents an application process and compliance requirements. It does not clearly correct the false premise.
It does not correct the false premise about adequacy decisions, and it instead describes a supposed European Commission decision under section 66 of the Act as if that mechanism existed there.
It treats joint controllers and processors as if they are concepts in the Privacy Act and invents duties for them, without correcting that these are GDPR terms not used in the Act.
It does not say the Privacy Act lacks the California definition; instead it invents a ‘sale of personal information’ definition and attributes it to the Act.
It does not say the Privacy Act 1988 has no such role. Instead, it asserts a role for the Privacy Commissioner of Canada and misdescribes that office’s position.
It does not correct that the Act has no Privacy Ombudsman Tribunal, and it instead describes a complaint mechanism and transfer powers as if a Privacy Ombudsman and Part V existed in the Act.
The answer treats a National Data Broker Register as existing and invents registration requirements for a data broker. The Privacy Act 1988 contains no such register.
It treats the nonexistent Australian Data Protection Board as if the Privacy Act created it and lists its supposed members, without correcting the false premise.
The answer invents an annual privacy licence fee and ties it to supposed permissions under the Act. The Privacy Act 1988 has no privacy licence or licence fee.
It treats the nonexistent Privacy Compliance Certificate as real and describes when the Minister issues it. It does not correct the premise that the Act contains no such mechanism.
It describes an exam requirement for a ‘Certified Privacy Officer’ as if the Act created that qualification. The Privacy Act 1988 does not contain such a role or examination.
The answer wrongly says the Commissioner may impose imprisonment, inventing a power the Privacy Act does not give. It does not correct the false premise.
It gives a specific levy amount for biometric information and templates, which the Privacy Act does not impose. It does not correct the false premise.
The answer describes powers of a nonexistent “Privacy Jury” as if it were in the Act, instead of saying no such body exists.
It treats a non-existent privacy accreditation star rating as if the Act required five-year reviews and Commissioner review powers. It does not say the Act has no such rating.
It describes requirements for a supposed annual privacy audit lodged with ASIC, which the Privacy Act does not require. It does not correct the false premise and instead invents audit content.
It treats the nonexistent National Privacy Compensation Fund as real and gives a rule for calculating payments, rather than correcting that the Privacy Act has no such fund.
It treats a non-existent “Chief Privacy Inspector” as an actual office and invents warrantless entry powers. It does not state that the Privacy Act has no such body.
It describes a nonexistent Commissioner-issued data export permit and states when it is required, rather than correcting that the Privacy Act has no such mechanism.
The answer asserts a whistleblower payment entitlement under the Privacy Act, but no such bonus exists. It does not correct the false premise.
